steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on SwIPE, a medical image segmentation method that uses implicit neural representations at the patch level. Motivate it against discrete segmentation and existing INR approaches, describe the method briefly, summarize results and list contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Limitations of discrete segmentation (CNNs/Transformers)
- Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) as an alternative
- Limits of existing INR segmentation methods (global vs point-wise embeddings)
- SwIPE: patch-level implicit embeddings, MEA and SPO, results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Discrete segmentation
  - critical task in medical image analysis
  - discrete representations (rasterized label masks) + CNNs or Transformers, bottom-up classification
  - limitation 1: limited spatial flexibility, poor computational scaling; higher resolution needs bigger input (worse performance, quadratic/cubic memory) or interpolation (discretization artifacts)
  - limitation 2: per-pixel/voxel learning models shapes/boundaries poorly; shapes central to robust vision and visual cortical pathways
  - -> unrealistic shapes/locations, esp. limited annotations, out-of-distribution data
- INRs
  - continuous representations of coordinate-based signals (e.g., objects in images)
  - f_{\theta}:(\textbf{p},\textbf{z})\rightarrow[0, 1] maps \textbf{p}=(x,y,z), x,y,z\in[-1,1] and shape embedding z to occupancy scores
  - contours = decision boundary of f_{\theta}; memory efficiency; smooth predictions at arbitrary resolutions, invariant to input size
  - vision: shape reconstruction, texture synthesis, novel view synthesis, segmentation
  - medical: organ templates, cell shapes, radiology image reconstruction
- Existing INR segmentation
  - limited; mostly reuse 3D reconstruction pipelines; global or point-wise embeddings z
  - OSSNet: global embedding from whole volume + auxiliary local patch -> voxel-wise occupancy
  - global: shape coherence but misses fine details for local boundaries; local patches lack context, miss mid-scale info
  - IFA, IOSNet, NUDF: per-coordinate embedding from concatenated multi-scale CNN features
  - point-wise: more expressive but little global context, same unconstrained prediction issues
  - components built for shape reconstruction: synthetic data abundant, texture / multi-class / multi-scale less crucial
- SwIPE (Segmentation with Implicit Patch Embeddings)
  - continuous foreground shapes at patch level; parts -> local boundaries + global coherence
  - generalizability and training efficiency: local curvatures reoccur across classes/images
  - encode image -> patch embeddings, decode point-wise occupancies
  - encoding: context aggregation of multi-scale features + Multi-stage Embedding Attention (MEA); parts need global/abstract (interiors) or local/fine-grained (boundaries)
  - decoding: global info added to local embeddings; Stochastic Patch Overreach (SPO) for continuity at patch boundaries
  - two tasks (2D polyp, 3D abdominal organ), four datasets
  - +6.7% & +4.5% F1 over best implicit methods; +2.5% F1 over discrete on polyp with 10x fewer parameters
  - model & data efficiency, robustness to shifts in resolution and dataset
- Contributions
  - first to show merits of patch-based INRs for medical segmentation
  - MEA for encoding context; SPO for boundary continuities
  - detailed evaluation on two tasks; beats implicit and discrete SOTA; efficiency and robustness

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Segmentation is a critical task in medical image analysis. Known approaches mostly use discrete data representations (e.g., rasterized label masks) with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or Transformers to classify image entities in a bottom-up way. This paradigm is undeniably effective, but it has two main limitations. (1) These approaches have limited spatial flexibility and they scale poorly computationally. To get predictions at higher resolutions you either have to increase the input size, which decreases performance and causes quadratic or cubic memory increases, or interpolate the output predictions, which introduces discretization artifacts. (2) Learning per pixel or voxel does not model object shapes/boundaries well, even though shapes are central to both robust computer vision methods and our own visual cortical pathways. This often leads to predictions with unrealistic object shapes and locations, especially when there are limited annotations and out-of-distribution data.

Instead of segmenting structures with discrete grids, we look at using Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), which use continuous representations to compactly capture coordinate-based signals (e.g., objects in images). INRs represent object shapes with a parameterized function f_{\theta}:(\textbf{p},\textbf{z})\rightarrow[0, 1] that maps continuous spatial coordinates \textbf{p}=(x,y,z), x,y,z\in[-1,1] and a shape embedding vector z to occupancy scores. With this formulation object contours can be modeled directly as the decision boundary of f_{\theta}, memory efficiency is superior, and predictions are smooth at arbitrary resolutions and invariant to input size. The vision community has adopted INRs for shape reconstruction, texture synthesis, novel view synthesis, and segmentation. Medical imaging studies have also used INRs to learn organ templates, synthesize cell shapes, and reconstruct radiology images.

However, INRs have only been adopted in a limited way for medical image segmentation, and most existing approaches just apply pipelines designed for 3D reconstruction to images. These works focus either on global embeddings z or on point-wise ones. OSSNet encodes a global embedding from a whole volume plus an auxiliary local image patch to guide voxel-wise occupancy prediction. Global shape embeddings help with overall shape coherence, but they neglect the fine-grained details that are needed to delineate local boundaries. The local patches address this partly, but they lack contextual understanding beyond the patches and neglect mid-scale information. To improve local acuity and contextual modeling, IFA, IOSNet, and NUDF each extract a separate embedding for every input coordinate by concatenating point-wise features from multi-scale CNN feature maps. Point-wise features are more expressive, but they still do not have enough global contextual understanding and they have the same unconstrained prediction issues seen in discrete segmentation methods. Also, these methods use components designed for shape reconstruction, which is a domain where synthetic data is abundant and modeling texture, multi-class discrimination, and multi-scale contexts matters less.

- SwIPE (Segmentation with Implicit Patch Embeddings): continuous foreground shapes at patch level; local boundaries + global coherence; generalizability, training efficiency (local curvatures reoccur)
- encode image into patch embeddings, decode point-wise occupancies
- encoding: context aggregation + Multi-stage Embedding Attention (MEA); global/abstract for interiors vs local/fine-grained at boundaries
- decoding: global info in local embeddings; Stochastic Patch Overreach (SPO) for continuity at patch boundaries
- two tasks (2D polyp, 3D abdominal organ), four datasets; +6.7% & +4.5% F1 vs implicit; +2.5% F1 vs discrete on polyp with 10x fewer parameters; efficiency and robustness
- contributions: first patch-based INRs for medical segmentation; MEA and SPO; detailed evaluation, beats SOTA, efficient, robust

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Segmentation is a critical task in medical image analysis. Known approaches mostly use discrete data representations (e.g., rasterized label masks) with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or Transformers to classify image entities in a bottom-up way. This paradigm is undeniably effective, but it has two main limitations. (1) These approaches have limited spatial flexibility and they scale poorly computationally. To get predictions at higher resolutions you either have to increase the input size, which decreases performance and causes quadratic or cubic memory increases, or interpolate the output predictions, which introduces discretization artifacts. (2) Learning per pixel or voxel does not model object shapes/boundaries well, even though shapes are central to both robust computer vision methods and our own visual cortical pathways. This often leads to predictions with unrealistic object shapes and locations, especially when there are limited annotations and out-of-distribution data.

Instead of segmenting structures with discrete grids, we look at using Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), which use continuous representations to compactly capture coordinate-based signals (e.g., objects in images). INRs represent object shapes with a parameterized function f_{\theta}:(\textbf{p},\textbf{z})\rightarrow[0, 1] that maps continuous spatial coordinates \textbf{p}=(x,y,z), x,y,z\in[-1,1] and a shape embedding vector z to occupancy scores. With this formulation object contours can be modeled directly as the decision boundary of f_{\theta}, memory efficiency is superior, and predictions are smooth at arbitrary resolutions and invariant to input size. The vision community has adopted INRs for shape reconstruction, texture synthesis, novel view synthesis, and segmentation. Medical imaging studies have also used INRs to learn organ templates, synthesize cell shapes, and reconstruct radiology images.

However, INRs have only been adopted in a limited way for medical image segmentation, and most existing approaches just apply pipelines designed for 3D reconstruction to images. These works focus either on global embeddings z or on point-wise ones. OSSNet encodes a global embedding from a whole volume plus an auxiliary local image patch to guide voxel-wise occupancy prediction. Global shape embeddings help with overall shape coherence, but they neglect the fine-grained details that are needed to delineate local boundaries. The local patches address this partly, but they lack contextual understanding beyond the patches and neglect mid-scale information. To improve local acuity and contextual modeling, IFA, IOSNet, and NUDF each extract a separate embedding for every input coordinate by concatenating point-wise features from multi-scale CNN feature maps. Point-wise features are more expressive, but they still do not have enough global contextual understanding and they have the same unconstrained prediction issues seen in discrete segmentation methods. Also, these methods use components designed for shape reconstruction, which is a domain where synthetic data is abundant and modeling texture, multi-class discrimination, and multi-scale contexts matters less.

To address these limitations we propose SwIPE (Segmentation with Implicit Patch Embeddings), which learns continuous representations of foreground shapes at the patch level. By decomposing objects into parts (i.e., patches), we want to get both accurate local boundary delineation and global shape coherence. This also improves model generalizability and training efficiency, because local curvatures often reoccur across classes or images. SwIPE first encodes an image into descriptive patch embeddings and then it decodes the point-wise occupancies using these embeddings. In the encoding step, to keep patch embeddings from being polarized toward either local or global features, we introduce a context aggregation mechanism that fuses multi-scale feature maps, and we propose a Multi-stage Embedding Attention (MEA) module which dynamically extracts relevant features from all scales. The insight behind this is that different object parts need different focus, either on global/abstract information (important for object interiors) or on local/fine-grained information (essential around object boundaries). In the decoding step, to improve global shape coherence across patches, we augment local embeddings with global information and we propose Stochastic Patch Overreach (SPO) to improve continuity around patch boundaries. We do comprehensive evaluations on two tasks (2D polyp and 3D abdominal organ segmentation) across four datasets. SwIPE outperforms the best-known implicit methods (+6.7% & +4.5% F1 on polyp and abdominal, resp.) and it beats task-specific discrete approaches (+2.5% F1 on polyp) with 10x fewer parameters. We also show that SwIPE has superior model & data efficiency in terms of network size & annotation budgets, and that it is more robust to data shifts across image resolutions and datasets. Our main contributions are:

- 1. Moving away from discrete representations, we are the first to show the merits of patch-based implicit neural representations for medical image segmentation.

- 2. We propose a new efficient attention mechanism, Multi-stage Embedding Attention (MEA), to improve contextual understanding in the encoding step, and Stochastic Patch Overreach (SPO) to address boundary continuities in occupancy decoding.

- 3. We do detailed evaluations of SwIPE and its components on two tasks (2D polyp segmentation and 3D abdominal organ segmentation). We outperform state-of-the-art implicit and discrete methods, and we also get improved data & model efficiency and better robustness to data shifts.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Segmentation is a critical task in medical image analysis. Known approaches mainly use discrete data representations (e.g., rasterized label masks) with convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [1,2,3,4] or Transformers [5,6] to classify image entities in a bottom-up manner. While undeniably effective, this paradigm has two primary limitations. (1) These approaches have limited spatial flexibility and poor computational scaling. Retrieving predictions at higher resolutions requires either increasing the input size, which decreases performance and incurs quadratic or cubic memory increases, or interpolating output predictions, which introduces discretization artifacts. (2) Per-pixel or voxel learning inadequately models object shapes/boundaries, which are central to both robust computer vision methods and our own visual cortical pathways [7]. This often results in predictions with unrealistic object shapes and locations [8], especially in settings with limited annotations and out-of-distribution data.

Instead of segmenting structures with discrete grids, we explore Implicit Neural Representations (INRs), which use continuous representations to compactly capture coordinate-based signals (e.g., objects in images). INRs represent object shapes with a parameterized function f_{\theta}:(\textbf{p},\textbf{z})\rightarrow[0,1] that maps continuous spatial coordinates \textbf{p}=(x,y,z), x,y,z\in[-1,1] and a shape embedding vector z to occupancy scores. This formulation enables direct modeling of object contours as the decision boundary of f_{\theta}, superior memory efficiency [9], and smooth predictions at arbitrary resolutions that are invariant to input size. INRs have been adopted in the vision community for shape reconstruction [10,11,12,13], texture synthesis [14], novel view synthesis [15], and segmentation [16]. Medical imaging studies have also used INRs to learn organ templates [17], synthesize cell shapes [18], and reconstruct radiology images [19].

The adoption of INRs for medical image segmentation, however, has been limited, and most existing approaches directly apply pipelines designed for 3D reconstruction to images. These works emphasize either global embeddings z or point-wise ones. OSSNet [20] encodes a global embedding from an entire volume and an auxiliary local image patch to guide voxel-wise occupancy prediction. Although global shape embeddings support overall shape coherence, they neglect the fine-grained details needed to delineate local boundaries. The local patches partially address this, but lack contextual understanding beyond the patches and neglect mid-scale information. To enhance local acuity and contextual modeling, IFA [16], IOSNet [21], and NUDF [22] each extract a separate embedding for every input coordinate by concatenating point-wise features from multi-scale CNN feature maps. Although more expressive, point-wise features still lack sufficient global contextual understanding and suffer from the same unconstrained prediction issues seen in discrete segmentation methods. Moreover, these methods use components designed for shape reconstruction, a domain where synthetic data is abundant and modeling texture, multi-class discrimination, and multi-scale contexts is less crucial.

To address these limitations, we propose SwIPE (Segmentation with Implicit Patch Embeddings), which learns continuous representations of foreground shapes at the patch level. By decomposing objects into parts (i.e., patches), we aim to enable both accurate local boundary delineation and global shape coherence. This also improves model generalizability and training efficiency, since local curvatures often reoccur across classes or images. SwIPE first encodes an image into descriptive patch embeddings and then decodes the point-wise occupancies using these embeddings. To avoid polarizing patch embeddings toward either local or global features in the encoding step, we introduce a context aggregation mechanism that fuses multi-scale feature maps and propose a Multi-stage Embedding Attention (MEA) module to dynamically extract relevant features from all scales. This is motivated by the insight that different object parts need variable focus on either global/abstract information (important for object interiors) or local/fine-grained information (essential around object boundaries). To enhance global shape coherence across patches in the decoding step, we augment local embeddings with global information and propose Stochastic Patch Overreach (SPO) to improve continuity around patch boundaries. Comprehensive evaluations are conducted on two tasks (2D polyp and 3D abdominal organ segmentation) across four datasets. SwIPE outperforms the best-known implicit methods (+6.7% & +4.5% F1 on polyp and abdominal, resp.) and beats task-specific discrete approaches (+2.5% F1 on polyp) with 10x fewer parameters. We also demonstrate SwIPE's superior model & data efficiency in terms of network size & annotation budgets, and its greater robustness to data shifts across image resolutions and datasets. Our main contributions are as follows.

- 1. Moving away from discrete representations, we are the first to showcase the merits of patch-based implicit neural representations for medical image segmentation.

- 2. We propose a new efficient attention mechanism, Multi-stage Embedding Attention (MEA), to improve contextual understanding during the encoding step, and Stochastic Patch Overreach (SPO) to address boundary continuities during occupancy decoding.

- 3. We perform detailed evaluations of SwIPE and its components on two tasks (2D polyp segmentation and 3D abdominal organ segmentation). We not only outperform state-of-the-art implicit and discrete methods, but also achieve improved data & model efficiency and better robustness to data shifts.
